title: Deterministic client resume & graceful-degrade PRD — pagination, streaming, retries
creator: Morgan Chen
description: Product requirements for a convergent SDK surface that enables deterministic pagination cursors, resumable streaming, and predictable graceful degradation across Python, TypeScript, and Go clients. The goal is to give engineering teams clear contracts for resume semantics, idempotent retry behavior, and downgrade fallbacks so production apps can recover from partial failures without data corruption or surprising UX regressions.
scope: Design and spec an SDK-level contract for deterministic cursors (opaque token) that allow exact continuation of paginated fetches across language SDKs and server-side rollouts.
Define resumable streaming handshake and checkpointing model to allow clients to reconnect and pick up where they left off for both server-stream and bidi stream semantics.
Specify retry idempotency keys and recommended default backoff policies for high-level SDK APIs (list, fetch, stream).
Provide language-specific examples and helper primitives for Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs.
Define acceptance tests and integration verification steps for the server and SDKs.
Provide migration guidance and deprecation windows for existing cursor/stream surfaces.
non_goals: Ship runtime-level server implementations — this PRD scopes the SDK contract only; server-side compatibility work tracked as ENG work.
Provide exhaustive transport-layer implementations for every edge-case (will provide canonical reference implementations only).
Change existing public API shapes beyond adding optional fields and helper overloads — we will avoid breaking changes for GA.
requirements: Deterministic Cursor Contract: server returns an opaque cursor token (base64) with each paginated response. Cursor must encode server-side version and sequence metadata. SDKs must treat token as opaque and not attempt to parse. Cursor invalidation must return a well-defined error code `cursor_invalid` with a recovery hint.

Resume Semantics for Streams: streaming responses must emit periodic checkpoint events (control frame) containing a resume_token and stable checkpoint offset. Clients reconnecting present resume_token to continue. If resume_token expired, server returns `resume_expired` and client must fallback to full request re-run.
Idempotent Retry Keys: APIs that mutate or create resources must accept an idempotency key header/parameter. SDK helper must auto-generate UUIDv4 keys when user doesn't supply one.
language_considerations: Python: provide 'resume()' coroutine helper on stream objects that accepts timeout and backoff config. Default retry policy: expo backoff with jitter, max attempts 5.
TypeScript: expose typed AsyncIterable for streaming with `.resume(token)` method; prefer streaming via WebSocket or HTTP/2; include helper that polyfills resume across transports.
Go: provide context-aware Resume(ctx, token) method returning a channel and an error stream; document goroutine safety and cancellation semantics.
api_examples: Python paginated iterator example: `for page in client.list_items(cursor=None, page_size=100): process(page)` — SDK exposes `Page.cursor` on each page object.
TS streaming resume example: `const s = client.streamMessages(req); await for await (const msg of s) { if (msg.checkpoint) token = msg.token } // later s.resume(token)`
Go idempotency: `id := client.NewIdempotencyKey(); resp, err := client.CreateResource(ctx, req, id)` — SDK auto-generates if `id` is empty.
acceptance_criteria: All three SDKs (Python/TS/Go) implement cursor passthrough surface and return `cursor` on Page objects or equivalent. Integration tests verify exact continuation semantics across server rollout variants.

Streaming clients emit resumable checkpoints at least every N seconds (configurable; default 15s) and provide `resume` helpers. Automated reconnection test reproduces mid-stream disconnect and validates no duplicate processed items beyond at-most-once/at-least-once trade-off documented.
Default retry/backoff is implemented and documented for each SDK; SDK tests assert retry stops after configured attempts and respects idempotency key usage for mutating endpoints.

Backward compatibility: existing consumer code using previous cursor tokens must either continue working (server accepts old tokens) or receive `cursor_invalid` with migration hints. Acceptance tests include a simulated server-side cursor format change and verify client error flow and migration guidance surfaced in logs.
Docs and examples published in the SDK repos and developer docs with migration guides and patterns for handling resume failures.
rollout_plan: Week 1: Finalize contract doc and publish canonical examples for Python/TS/Go. Share with core SDK owners and runtime teams.
Week 2: Engineering implements SDK helpers and stubbed tests; runtime team implements resume_token plumbing and error codes in staging.
Week 3: End-to-end integration tests in staging with simulated disconnects, cursor-rotation, and server rollouts. Fix interoperability issues.
Week 4: Canary release for SDK minor versions and controlled server rollout (10% traffic) while monitoring resume error rate and customer-facing logs.
Post-canary: Full rollout, deprecation notices for incompatible cursor formats, and retroactive bugfix window.
open_questions: Token format: how much versioning metadata should server embed vs. keeping token minimal? (security team prefers minimal surface).
Checkpoint frequency trade-off: default 15s recommended but need perf experiment — what is acceptable extra control-frame overhead for 99th percentile latency?
How to express at-most-once vs at-least-once guarantees across transports in API docs to avoid misleading expectations?
Do we require SDKs to buffer unacknowledged messages locally to avoid duplicates, or is that left to customers?
decisions: Adopt opaque base64 cursor tokens with server-side version prefix — server will include `v=` metadata inside token but SDKs will treat it as opaque.
Default checkpoint interval set to 15s with per-stream override; engineering will measure and revisit based on P99 latency impact.
SDKs will provide helper defaults but surface configuration to let users opt into stricter semantics (e.g., exactly-once helpers for idempotent operations).
